text: Welcome to This is My Architecture. We are in Mumbai. I'm Gaurav and I've got AB with me. Hi, AB.
Hi, Gaurav. AB, tell me something about HDFC Life. So HDFC Life is the second largest insurance
provider in India, life insurance provider in India, and it has been in India for the past 19
years and we have been reaching out to all of the customers across India and providing
life insurance for them.
Lovely. And we are discussing the second time about data lakes. Tell me how it has evolved
since.
So data lake traditionally is a basic requirement for all of the companies out right now and
within this time and era we would need something which would work on a real-time basis more
than something which is running on a delayed basis. So we looked at our existing data lake
and found that it is high time for an upgrade and we need something which works more real-time
and on an event-driven basis to mimic the real world.
Right. And in a large enterprise, I'm sure that the source systems are not so easy to
deal with. So tell me about what the source systems are and how do you take the data from
there?
So our, we have a good legacy. So we have AS400 and we have the latest possible databases
right to, up to DynamoDB. So we have different dissipated data sources along with flat files
and multiple, multitudes or different types of data which we have to bring into play. And
that's where all of these boxes comes in.
So how does the data flow in the architecture?
So what we have is all of the dissipated data sources and of course we have a direct
connect pipe which is built in to pull in all of these data sources into our AWS infrastructure.
Uh-huh.
For when we have all of the data coming in, we have DMS sitting over here which basically
is the feed for pulling all of the data from the separate sources and into our AWS landscape
which in this case being DynamoDB.
Lovely. So you're using database migration as a service and getting data into DynamoDB.
You've got the data layered into raw L1, L2. Can you tell us about those please?
So traditionally layers are built into any data warehouse or data lake and they have a different
purpose. In this case, the layers which we have in place are not to kind of separate the
data but to kind of personify each of the layers into some meaning to it. Now each of these layers
have a certain meaning and working from bottom to top. Raw is just a mimicry of existing sources
but all of them in one place.
Uh-huh.
L1 builds the user persona on top of raw and L2 enriches those user personas with behaviors
and attributes to it.
Brilliant. And interesting choice of a database you've got for staging. You're using DynamoDB.
Can you explain the choice of that?
So traditionally you wouldn't expect DynamoDB to be a choice for a data lake platform. But if you can
evaluate in terms of our requirements and the drive to kind of upgrade this into a real-time
driven architecture.
Uh-huh.
You will find that if you have lots and lots of transaction happening on again and again
repeatedly, you would need something which doesn't burden us in terms of cost. And when
you can evaluated the cost between DynamoDB and S3, we found that DynamoDB is actually
cheaper when it comes to a real-time driven architecture.
Lovely. And how does the event driven architecture work between DynamoDB and Lambdas?
So, DynamoDB within itself is actually packaging a lot of features and one of the best features
being the DynamoDB streams which is tightly coupled with Lambdas. So, when you have that
feature already in, it gives us two things. One, it gives you the event driven part.
Uh-huh.
And at the same time, it also gives you resilience because it also handles in error part where
everything errors out, it yet triggers in Lambda. So, you have the DynamoDB streams which then
have Lambdas being triggered and wherein all of the data processing happens between
intermittent layers. And Lambdas then push in those layers back to your L1 or L2 from
raw to L1 or L1 to L2. Interesting. So, can you give me an estimate in terms of how many
Lambda functions are we talking about? So, we have around 550 odd Lambdas which transfer the data
between raw to L1 and L1 to L2. Uh-huh.
And along with these Lambdas, we also have step functions which does further orchestrations
to build up multiple other, provide multiple other business objectives.
Cool. And I see that you still retained your S3 bucket data lake. So, can you walk us through
the reason for that existing in an event driven architecture?
Yes. So, when it comes to an event driven architecture, we know that 90 to 95 percent of it can be done
at the time. Uh-huh. Even when it comes to the remaining 5 percent bulk operation, we have managed
to build it using Lambdas and DynamoDB within the Lambdas and DynamoDB themselves. But what we are
missing out is in terms of an mistake which happens or an error which happens where a recovery is
required back into DynamoDB. We found that through experience that whenever a recoverability has to be
done, there is a cost involved in it. Uh-huh. And to figure out a way or when we kind of
build the options, we found S3 and Athena joint can become a good serverless recovery mechanism
to kind of rebuild any of our existing data lake platforms in case of errors.
Interesting. So, you are not burdening your source systems when you need to do a recovery.
Yes, that's correct. So, what happens is while the data is being pushed into DynamoDB,
at the same time it is also being pushed into S3. Uh-huh.
But all of the intermittent layers are not built. We only keep the data at the raw layer. And if at any point
we find an error in any one of the layer or any partial error in part of the layer, uh with say
within raw L1 was there was some business change and we need rebuild that layer. We use Athena, uh
as a to and fro data mechanism where we rebuild the layer within S3. And once the layer is built
within S3 using Athena, we again push that data back into DynamoDB.
It is brilliant way to get things done. So, where do you evolve from here? What comes next?
So, we have kind of evolved on this existing architecture from an architecture which was
running in a slight lag. Now, to use this new real time architecture we had to do two things.
One is to basically get everything which is the existing architecture onto the new one.
Uh-huh. Second is to get this real time knowledge which you are gathering out to the end customer.
And that being both internal and external, salespeople and our end customers. Now, what we found is
the existing machine learning pieces which are there out in the market, there are much more advancement
in terms of reinforcement learning and it's being actively used. Uh-huh. And we want to figure out and explore
how to get reinforcement learning within the life insurance industry. And we are evaluating
how to use uh tensorflow on AWS SageMaker to achieve this. And so, we see the road map to be really interesting.
Lovely. Abhi, thanks for coming. Appreciate you. Thank you.
Uh-huh. And thanks for watching this episode of This is My Architecture.
